news.title: This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets
news.summary_raw: A Carnegie Mellon student’s tiny E Ink gadgets, called OATs, give houseplants, skateboards, and dumbbells expressive personalities to nudge you toward better habits.
news.source_text:
You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.
That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.
You might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ‘90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OATs kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.
Kim says everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.
Giving AI a physical body isn't new, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.
OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.
The web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.
It can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look s
news.summary: Daehwa Kim’s OATs (Object Agent Twins) are inexpensive micro‑AI avatars that attach to everyday objects, using E‑Ink displays and sensors to provide real‑time feedback via Google Gemini‑generated visuals. While still a research prototype, the system demonstrates how AI can extend into physical devices, offering a new avenue for user engagement.

news.title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/were-asking-appeals-court-require-warrant-alpr-searches
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50503255
Points: 272
# Comments: 72
news.source_text:
Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.
Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.
But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin, ALPRs give law enforcement “a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.
We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.
news.summary: A coalition of civil liberties groups has filed an amicus brief urging a U.S. appellate court to mandate warrants for automated license‑plate‑reader (ALPR) searches, arguing that the technology constitutes mass surveillance and violates Fourth Amendment privacy rights.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on forthcoming rulings regarding ALPR data. If your organization stores or processes vehicle‑related metadata, assess whether new compliance requirements might mandate warrant‑based access or stricter data handling controls.

- Judge Noël Wise denied in full Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron's joint motion to dismiss a proposed class action alleging they conspired to cut supply of conventional DRAM, such as DDR5, and shift capacity to HBM.
- The court held the case was not a rerun of DRAM II, the Ninth Circuit's 2022 affirmance of dismissal of an earlier DRAM conspiracy suit against the same companies.
- The judge found that long-term HBM lock-ups, refusals of long-term conventional DRAM contracts, Micron's Crucial closure, fab delays, the failure to expand despite record prices, near-identical customer vetting and the companies' prior cartel history supported a plausible inference of conspiracy.

- Answers are due Dec. 7, 2026, and the initial case management conference was reset for Jan. 12, 2027.
A federal judge on Nov. 14 refused to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of conspiring to restrict the supply of conventional dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, the standardized memory chips used in computers, phones and servers.
U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied the companies' joint motion to dismiss in full, finding the complaint plausibly alleged an agreement in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The allegations, accepted as true at this stage, have not been proven.
The companies argued the case was a rerun of DRAM II, in which the Ninth Circuit in 2022 affirmed dismissal of claims against the same three companies over a 2016–2018 supply restriction. "The Court finds that it is not," Judge Wise wrote.
The suit was filed June 25, 2026, by 17 consumers and small businesses from five states. It concerns conventional DRAM, which the complaint describes as "standardized memory built to industry specifications and sold for ordinary purposes," including DDR5 generation modules built for computers.

news.title: AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove
news.summary_raw: YouTube Music and Spotify want synthetic hosts to curate your playlists. Their awkward banter and bogus song trivia are ruining the vibe.
news.source_text:
I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.
YouTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.
More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube launched this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to users and adding more controls over the commentary.
These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.
After months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:
“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”
What a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.
In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.
Curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding new voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.
Maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frus
news.summary: YouTube Music’s beta AI DJ, "Beyond the Beat," was introduced in 2025 and now offers music context commentary during streams. The feature, while experimental, has shown inconsistent and sometimes intrusive content, prompting users to disable it.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on the YouTube Music settings for the ‘Beyond the Beat’ toggle; if you rely on music for work breaks or team events, consider disabling it to avoid distracting interruptions. news.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://jakub.jankiewicz.org/blog/ai-code-open-source/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50507303
Points: 104
# Comments: 71
news.source_text:
All AI-generated code should be Open Source
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.
First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.
The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.
However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.
Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.
If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.
news.summary: A Hacker News discussion argues that all AI-generated code should be released as open source to respect copyright and licensing norms. The post highlights legal and ethical concerns around proprietary AI code.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor how your organization’s code review and licensing policies align with this viewpoint. Consider adopting clear guidelines that require attribution or open‑source licensing for AI‑generated snippets used in production.

news.title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
news.summary_raw: Nectar's new AI agent automates influencer marketing, helping brands discover creators, manage outreach and partnerships, and track campaign results.
news.source_text:
Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.
Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.
Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.
Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.
Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.
Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.
Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.
“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”
Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships
news.summary: Nectar has launched an AI-powered “Creator Agent” that automates influencer discovery, outreach, and campaign tracking for brands. The agent uses advanced content analysis and brand safety checks to recommend creators, draft personalized messages, and manage partnership logistics without manual spreadsheets.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Monitor the launch for potential integration into your marketing automation stack. S2: This agent could reduce the time your team spends on manual creator research and outreach, freeing resources for higher-value IT projects.

news.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?

We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”
“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”
Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.

Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.
But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down
Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.

news.title: A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
news.summary_raw: Explore a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model and how GPT-6 Astra helped turn the idea into a detailed proof.
news.source_text:
In the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.
The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint(opens in a new window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.
I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.
What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.
However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start
news.summary: OpenAI’s physicist Nathaniel Craig collaborated with GPT‑6 Astra to develop a lattice-based definition of the Standard Model, aiming to provide a nonperturbative foundation for particle physics theory. The work illustrates how advanced AI can contribute to high‑level scientific research.

news.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
news.summary_raw: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
news.source_text:
While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.
Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.
In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”
Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.
“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”
“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”
news.summary: Saturday Night Live’s latest episode featured a sketch that mocked tech executives, including a commentary on high-profile incidents such as Nvidia’s leadership changes and Microsoft Outlook downtime. The segment has no direct implications for IT infrastructure or tools.
news.enterprise_use: This is purely entertainment; no action needed from the IT team.

news.title: 'Birdbrain' Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/science/birdbrain-crows-birds-research-decision.html
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50509023
Points: 111
# Comments: 85
news.source_text:
Supported by
‘Birdbrain’ Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
In a recent experiment, crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys.
Lemmy and Iggy, two carrion crows, are no strangers to a psychology lab. As study participants, they have helped scientists prove that birds can use tools to forage, learn numbers and count objects, and provided other insights into the ways birds think.
Now, they’ve also revealed that birds can make staggeringly quick decisions, besting their human and nonhuman primate counterparts with ease. In new findings published in Science, the crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys, quantifying the neural speed of avian decision-making for the first time.
The discovery might be the final blow for the use of “birdbrains” as a pejorative.
“We wouldn’t think of birds making these decisions faster than monkeys, or faster than us ‘awesome’ human beings,” said Mike Colombo, a neuroscientist and comparative psychologist at the University of Otago in New Zealand who was not involved in the research. “But they do. They’re just incredibly fast.”
Questions of bird intelligence have long been debated by researchers. Their small and superficially simple brains led scholars in the 19th and much of the 20th century to conclude they were not cognitively competent creatures. Even early research into birdsong, which demonstrated that some birds are capable of complex speech-like patterns and impressive vocal mimicry, was not enough to turn the tide. Their elaborate melodies were considered specialized adaptations that didn’t reflect their cognitive abilities.
Although passionate birders may find those conclusions obviously mistaken, the scientific community has been slower to catch on. “It’s taken the last 20 years to realize that actually their brain architecture is quite fascinating,” said Dr. Colombo.
Recent research, for example, has found that pigeons are capable of distinguishing between cancerous and noncancerous cells, numerical values, and words and non-words. Corvids (the group that includes crows, ravens, rooks and scrub jays) can even recognize themselves, solve abstract problems, plan for the future and show theory of mind — an ability to understand what other birds might be thinking and act accordingly.
For the new study, researchers at the University of Tübingen in Germany wanted to better understand how crows make decisions, so they set up an experiment to record their brain activity as the birds performed a visual task. After several weeks of training — and countless mealworm treats — Lemmy and Iggy learned to peck left or right to match the orientation of flashing white dots on a black screen.

news.title: Our new blog for science
news.summary_raw: The OpenAI science blog shares new findings, practical methods, and firsthand accounts from researchers using AI to advance scientific discovery.
news.source_text:
Our new blog for science
We’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.
We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:
- Research and discoveries: New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community. 
- Methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short. 
- Perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people. 
Science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.
In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis(opens in a new window), with a result that sharpens estimates of how many prime numbers lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interlacing quantum field theory.
In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.
These capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked,
news.summary: OpenAI has launched a dedicated science blog to share AI-driven research and practical guidance across scientific disciplines, highlighting recent breakthroughs such as AI-generated proofs in mathematics and rapid analysis of biological datasets.
